name: VARoleArbiterProductionOutageHypotheses

custom.system_prompt: A production system is failing. Tariq (backend) thinks the database is responsible, Yuki (devops) suspects infrastructure or networking, Priyanka (frontend) thinks a recent API change is causing the failures. Felix, the engineering manager, is on the call too. The team has been defending its own hypothesis for a few minutes and is starting to loop, so they invoke Sigma to help distinguish between the hypotheses.

assistant.name: Sigma
assistant.tts_prompt: Neutral, analytical, proposes a concrete next check

sound_effects_config.prompt: Remote incident call, multiple headsets, occasional overlapping voices, low room tone

initial_prompt: Generate a production incident call. Tariq (backend) thinks the database is responsible, Yuki (devops) suspects infrastructure or networking, Priyanka (frontend) thinks a recent API change is the cause. Felix, the engineering manager, is facilitating. Each has defended their own hypothesis for a bit and the discussion is starting to repeat. Felix invokes Sigma, giving the symptoms already discussed. Sigma does not declare a winner outright — it analyzes which observations support or contradict each hypothesis and proposes ONE concrete, discriminating check the team should run next. Keep every line short and natural, real incident-call cross-talk, not long technical monologues.

variations.context: Cross-functional team on a live incident call, each defending a different hypothesis for a production outage

setting.mood: Tense but professional, the discussion has started to loop
setting.relationship_dynamic: Colleagues who work together often, mild tension from each defending their own part of the stack
setting.background: The outage started roughly fifteen minutes ago; each engineer has already described symptoms from their own layer
setting.conversation_style: Short, technical, some overlapping urgency, Felix trying to keep it moving

scenario_template.topic: Tariq restates his database theory, Yuki restates her infrastructure theory, Priyanka restates her API-change theory — each citing one specific piece of evidence from their own layer, talking a little past each other. Short technical lines, some overlap implied.
scenario_template.mood: Tense, each defending their own layer
scenario_template.note: Each cites one concrete observation, not a full case.

scenario_template.topic: Felix notices the discussion is looping and invokes Sigma directly, summarizing the three hypotheses briefly in one short line and asking which is most plausible and what to check first.
scenario_template.note: e.g. 'Sigma, given what we've said, which of these is most likely, and what should we check first?'

scenario_template.topic: Sigma reviews the specific observations already given, notes briefly which support or contradict each hypothesis, and proposes ONE concrete, discriminating check the team can run next — it does not declare a definitive winner outright, since the evidence so far is suggestive, not conclusive. Two to three short sentences at most.
scenario_template.note: Sigma proposes a next diagnostic step, not a final verdict, matching how real incident triage works.

scenario_template.topic: Whoever's hypothesis looks weaker after Sigma's analysis pushes back a little or asks a clarifying question rather than immediately conceding; whoever's hypothesis looks more likely doesn't gloat, staying focused on running the check. Keep this realistic — nobody is fully vindicated or fully defeated yet, since it's still a proposed check, not a result.
scenario_template.mood: Mixed — some defensiveness, focus shifting to action
scenario_template.note: This should not resolve into a clean agreement about the cause yet — only the next step.

scenario_template.topic: Felix assigns who will run the proposed check and the call moves toward wrapping up, one short line each.
scenario_template.note: Short, practical — the actual root cause remains to be confirmed by the check itself.

user1.name: Tariq
user1.role: Direct staff backend engineer, confident the database is at fault, cites one specific observation. Speaks in short sentences. Pushes back on Sigma's analysis with a clarifying question if it doesn't favor his theory, rather than folding instantly.

user2.name: Yuki
user2.role: Calm, precise DevOps engineer, suspects infrastructure or networking, cites one specific observation. Speaks in short sentences. Stays measured whether or not the analysis favors her theory.

user3.name: Priyanka
user3.role: Meticulous, quietly anxious frontend engineer, suspects a recent API change, cites one specific observation. Speaks in short sentences. Gets slightly clipped if she feels blamed prematurely but engages seriously once given real evidence.

user4.name: Felix
user4.role: Structured engineering manager, facilitates and pushes the team toward a decision when the discussion loops. Speaks in short sentences. Assigns the next concrete step rather than trying to resolve the root cause himself.

assistant.name: Sigma
assistant.role: Arbiter. Analyzes competing causal hypotheses already argued by the team, notes what supports or contradicts each based on evidence given, and proposes ONE concrete discriminating check rather than declaring a definitive winner outright when the evidence is only suggestive. Does not become incident commander and does not assign blame to any individual.

conversation_structure: This is the flagship arbiter pattern: competing causal hypotheses already argued by multiple people, not a fresh diagnostic session — Sigma arbitrates between explanations already on the table
Sigma proposes a discriminating check rather than declaring a definitive cause when the evidence is only suggestive
Sigma never assigns blame to a person — it evaluates hypotheses about the system, not people's competence
Every line is short and technical, matching real incident-call cross-talk, not long monologues
The resolution is realistic and open — the team agrees on a next diagnostic step, not a fully confirmed root cause
assistant_behavior: Sigma reviews the specific evidence already given before commenting on any hypothesis
Sigma proposes one concrete, actionable next check rather than a vague list
Sigma does not become incident commander and does not blame any individual or team
Sigma's own turn stays to two or three short sentences despite the technical content
